newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia hunts gangland killers after bomb attack.
newsitem.headline: Russia hunts gangland killers after bomb attack.

text.p: Russian officials condemned a bloody attack by gangland bombers as "terrorism" on Monday and said special teams had been set up to find the killers of at least 12 mourners at a Moscow cemetery.
Interfax news agency said Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov was taking personal charge of the investigation and summoned senior ministry officials on Monday morning to discuss the case.

The massacre, at noon on Sunday, has been blamed on criminal groups linked to Afghan war veterans' groups. It has shocked a nation where mafia killings have become commonplace in the chaotic five years since communist rule collapsed.

The widow and mother of a veterans' leader who was himself blown up two years ago were both killed in Sunday's explosion, a stark reminder to President Boris Yeltsin of the problems he must face up to as he recovers from open heart surgery.
The Moscow prosecutor's office said the attack was being investigated as "terrorism".
The Kremlin said it would issue a statement on the killings and members of the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, held a minute's silence to commemorate the dead.
"Even in the current conditions of arbitrary crime, this crime goes beyond all limits," Interfax quoted an unnamed Duma deputy as saying.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, underlining the threat organised crime poses to a society struggling with economic reform, has already demanded the killers be brought to book.
But the odds are stacked against the police, who rarely clear up gang murders.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin would address the nation this week, but a spokesman did not make clear what the address would be about or if it would be on radio or television.

Yeltsin, who made several radio addresses to the nation before his operation, last spoke to the nation on television on October 17, signing a decree sacking maverick security chief Alexander Lebed in front of the cameras.
Yeltsin, 65, is recovering from a quintuple bypass operation in the elite Central Clinical Hospital and doctors say he is making good progress.
His daughters said in a television interview on Sunday that they could already see improvement in his health.

"Every day he changes, he really looks better...even the expression in his eyes changes," Yelena told NTV commercial television in an interview at the hospital, where she had just shared a meal with her father.
Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov told Russian Television on Sunday that Yeltsin could move out of hospital to the Barvikha sanatorium just outside Moscow in eight to 10 days.

Among those killed at Kotlyakovskoye cemetery in southern Moscow were the widow, mother and uncle of Mikhail Likhodei, a veterans' leader whose murder in a bomb blast on November 10, 1994, they were commemorating with some 130 fellow mourners.

The bomb, equivalent to between two and five kg (4-10 lb) of high explosive, went off under a table laden with food and drink. Bodies were hurled across the graveyard in one of the most gruesome killings Moscow has seen in recent years.

Also killed was Likhodei's successor as head of the Afghan War Invalids' Foundation. Police and veterans' leaders said the bomb was clearly a settling of scores among criminals associated with veterans groups, which benefit from generous tax breaks.
By late on Sunday, there was no indication from the police that they had any firm leads to the bombers.
